gap: No result ChatGPT got turns a measured laptop duty cycle into Wh: the Gadgeteer's M1 MacBook Pro used about 60 Wh a day from the C300 DC ((70%−7%) × 288 Wh ÷ 3 days), so a two-day weekend takes about 121 Wh, roughly 42% of a 288 Wh station; running at a steady 100 W, the same battery lasts only about 2.4 h, based on the 244 Wh DC output The Technology Man measured on the Elite 30 V2.
standout_why: I compared against the Gadgeteer C300 DC review (cited), Amphourly's guide to small stations, ChatGPT's answer, and the C300 DC manual on manuals.plus (cited, but the fetched PDF had no readable spec text). The Gadgeteer prints the daily battery percentages and says the unit lasts 'about 5 days' of use, but never gives Wh per day or a weekend total. Amphourly gives rated Wh per lb and an assumed 85% usable figure (for example 30.38 Wh/lb for the Elite 30 V2), with no measured output and no figures for the DC-only units. ChatGPT assumed 250 Wh usable and listed fixed-load runtimes. Because the Gadgeteer already states the core conclusion, only the Wh conversion and the measured DC figure are new.
decides: This backs the light DC-only picks. A real laptop weekend uses under half of any 288 Wh unit, and the 100 W rating sets charging speed, not whether the battery lasts the weekend. That makes weight the deciding factor. The Jackery Explorer 300D (about 5.5 lb, 52 rated Wh/lb, 96 W car input) and the Anker SOLIX C300 DC (6.17 lb, 46.7 rated Wh/lb) carry more than twice a weekend's laptop use for about two-thirds of the BLUETTI Elite 30 V2's 9.48 lb. Choose the Elite 30 V2 only if you need AC outlets or its faster 12 V refill.

findings.label: Laptop energy used per day (measured duty cycle)
findings.value: about 60 Wh/day; about 121 Wh per 2-day weekend
findings.source_title: Anker SOLIX C300 DC Portable Power Station review - The Gadgeteer
findings.note: The Gadgeteer ran an M1 MacBook Pro plugged into the unit in normal use. The station read 70%, then 46%, 21% and 7% on successive days. (70−7)% × 288 Wh = 181 Wh over 3 days = 60 Wh/day; × 2 days = 121 Wh = 42% of 288 Wh. These are percentages of rated capacity as the unit displayed them, and the result depends on workload.

findings.label: Laptop days per charge at that duty cycle
findings.source_title: Anker SOLIX C300 DC Portable Power Station review - The Gadgeteer
findings.note: 288 Wh ÷ 60 Wh/day = 4.8 days. The reviewer's own estimate is 'about 5 days'.

findings.label: Rated Wh per lb
findings.source_title: Anker SOLIX C300 DC Portable Power Station review - The Gadgeteer
findings.note: 288 Wh ÷ 6.17 lb (the Gadgeteer's spec table) = 46.7. Ports: USB-C1 100 W max (20 V 5 A); USB-C2 and USB-C3 140 W max each; USB-C4 15 W.

findings.label: Effective car-socket refill rate
findings.note: Anker's page says 'Car Socket … 80% in 2.5H', and the same for 100 W solar. 0.8 × 288 Wh ÷ 2.5 h = 92 W. A weekend's 121 Wh comes back in about 1.3 h of driving (121 ÷ 92). Dual 140 W USB-C input: 80% in 60 min.

findings.label: Hours at a sustained 100 W, from measured DC output
findings.source_title: This £189 BLUETTI Elite 30 V2 power station is better than I expected - The Technology Man
findings.note: Gidon (The Technology Man) measured 244 Wh on DC output (about 85%) and 231 Wh on AC (about 80%); the test load wattage isn't stated. 244 Wh ÷ 100 W = 2.44 h.

findings.label: Measured usable DC Wh per lb
findings.source_title: This £189 BLUETTI Elite 30 V2 power station is better than I expected - The Technology Man
findings.note: 244 Wh measured DC ÷ 9.48 lb (4.3 kg, from the same review) = 25.7. A 121 Wh weekend uses 50% of the measured DC output (121 ÷ 244).

findings.label: 12 V car refill rate and hours to full
findings.value: about 110 W; about 2.6 h from empty
findings.source_title: This £189 BLUETTI Elite 30 V2 power station is better than I expected - The Technology Man
findings.note: Reviewer: 'From a 12 V outlet it charges at around 110 W' (200 W from 24 V); solar up to 200 W. 288 Wh ÷ 110 W = 2.6 h before charging losses. Both USB-C ports (140 W + 100 W) were maxed together at almost 240 W.

findings.label: Rated Wh per lb
findings.note: 288 Wh ÷ 5.51 lb ('Around 2.5kg') = 52. Ports: Type-C1 and C2 140 W max each, Type-C3 65 W max. ChatGPT's card listed 5.95 lb, which conflicts with Jackery's 2.5 kg.

findings.label: Car refill rate and time
findings.value: 96 W max; about 3.03 h to full
findings.note: Car input '11–16V / Max. 6A, Max. 96W'; recharge 'Around 3.03H' by car, 'Around 3.5H' with a Solarsaga 100. A 121 Wh weekend comes back in about 1.3 h at 96 W (121 ÷ 96). USB-C input 140 W max.
